title: Moon surface imagery — how the layers work
intro_sentence: Zoom from the whole Moon down to a landing site and you are not looking at one picture but at six, from different cameras on different spacecraft, stacked on top of each other and swapped in as you get closer.
narrative_101: No single camera can show you both the whole Moon and a lunar module. A camera that sees the entire globe at once resolves a few kilometres per pixel; a camera sharp enough to pick out a descent stage sees a strip only a few kilometres wide. Mapping missions solve this the way online maps do on Earth: they keep several layers of imagery, each sharper and smaller than the one below, and show whichever one fits the view.

Think of it as a stack of slices hovering one above the other. The bottom slice is one image of the whole Moon. Each slice above covers less ground in more detail. At the very top you are standing on the surface, looking at the photographs the crews and landers took themselves.

Every slice is the work of a different mission, and together they took more than half a century. The first orbital maps were photographs on film, developed on board the Lunar Orbiter probes of 1966–67 and scanned for radio. [Clementine](app:/missions?id=clementine) mapped most of the Moon in digital multispectral images in 1994; Europe's [SMART-1](app:/missions?id=smart-1), China's [Chang'e 1](app:/missions?id=change1), India's [Chandrayaan-1](app:/missions?id=chandrayaan1) and Japan's Kaguya followed in the 2000s. The sharpest pictures in this app come from NASA's [Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter](app:/fleet?id=lro), at work since 2009.
body_paragraphs: Level 0 is the globe: a 4096-pixel global texture wrapped around the sphere. The Moon's equator is about 10,900 km long, so each pixel spans roughly 2.7 km — plenty from orbit, far too coarse to see where anyone landed. Level 1 is the context layer: around the site you have selected, a 400 km piece of the mosaic made by LRO's Wide Angle Camera, about 100 m per pixel, is draped over the globe at its true latitude and longitude. The Wide Angle Camera images a strip 60 km wide in seven colour bands; as the Moon turns beneath LRO's polar orbit, the strips add up to the whole globe, and the long shadows of low sunlight near the [terminator](planets/sub-solar-and-terminator) are what make craters stand out. The layer is drawn at true scale, takes its colour and brightness from the globe, and fades softly into it at the edges.

Level 2 is the regional view, 15 to 28 km of ground around the landing point. At most landers it comes from the Terrain Camera on Japan's Kaguya (SELENE) orbiter, which mapped nearly the whole Moon at about 10 m per pixel between 2007 and 2009. The Terrain Camera had two telescopes, one looking ahead and one behind, so every spot was seen twice from different angles and its height could be measured as well. At the six Apollo sites the regional view is a wider crop of the LRO mosaic used one level up. Level 3 is the detail view: 1 to 10 km around the lander from LRO's two Narrow Angle Cameras. Like most mapping cameras they are pushbroom cameras: a single line of pixels sweeps across the ground as the spacecraft moves, and the picture is built line by line. From LRO's low [orbit](orbits/orbit-regimes) they resolve about half a metre per pixel; here they are used as mosaics resampled to 5 m per pixel.

Level 4 is the route tiles. Along the [Apollo 16](app:/missions?id=apollo16) and [Apollo 17](app:/missions?id=apollo17) rover drives, the same Narrow Angle Cameras supply a string of 512 m tiles at 0.5 to 2 m per pixel, one at each stop and at regular steps along the drive. LRO's pictures of the Apollo sites show the descent stages and the lunar rovers, each with its shadow, where the crews left them. Level 5 is the panorama: the view from the ground. These are the photographs taken on the surface: the Apollo crews' Hasselblad frames, stitched into panoramas by contributors to the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal; the television cameras of [Lunokhod 1](app:/fleet?id=lunokhod-1) and [Lunokhod 2](app:/fleet?id=lunokhod-2); and the cameras of later landers and rovers such as [Yutu-2](app:/fleet?id=yutu-2) and [Pragyan](app:/fleet?id=pragyan).

How the layers meet. Each layer sits a hair above the one below, so the sharper image always wins where both exist, and each fades in by camera distance rather than popping in. At middle zooms the regional, detail and route patches are drawn larger than their true size so that you can see them at all; the imagery card says so. Zoom in further and the view switches to a flat patch at true scale. The imagery card in the corner always names the camera, the resolution and the licence of every layer on screen, and links to the source. The same orbiters also found water ice in permanently shadowed craters (see [lunar ice](planets/lunar-ice)), and the [regolith](planets/regolith) in their pictures is the ground the rovers drove on.

How the pictures reach you. The original crops are kept untouched in the project's archive. What your browser downloads are copies in several sizes, from 512 to 4096 pixels wide, and your device's quality setting picks the size: a phone on a slow connection gets the small one, a desktop on the cinematic setting the largest. Mars is mapped the same way, by other spacecraft: see [Mars surface imagery](planets/mars-surface-imagery).
diagram_caption: The Moon's six layers of imagery, from the whole-globe texture at the base to the photographs taken on the ground at the top, with the camera, resolution and ground covered by each.
